title: Richard III
author: William Shakespeare
setting: England at the end of the Wars of the Roses: London, the Tower, Pomfret, Salisbury and Bosworth Field
lengthNote: Around 3,600 lines — after Hamlet, the longest play in the Folio
openingLine: Now is the winter of our discontent Made glorious summer by this sun of York;
summary: A man tells the audience in the first forty lines exactly what he intends to do, and then does it while everyone on stage fails to notice. Richard's method is not secrecy but performance: he grieves for the brother he has imprisoned, refuses a crown he has arranged to be offered, and takes the audience into a confidence he offers nobody else. The play's problem is that the confidence works — and that it stops working in Act IV, when the jokes dry up and the women take over the stage.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Richard III
sourceText.note: The quarto and Folio texts differ substantially; line numbers here follow the traditional Globe numbering of the conflated text.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: It completes the sequence begun by the three Henry VI plays, and assumes an audience that knows them.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: A quarto printed by Valentine Simmes for Andrew Wise, with no author named. The 1598 second quarto adds Shakespeare's name.

atAGlance.label: Chief sources
atAGlance.note: Thomas More's hostile life of Richard reached Shakespeare through the Tudor chronicles, already shaped into a villain.

atAGlance.label: Two texts
atAGlance.note: The Folio text is longer and differs from the quarto tradition throughout; the relationship between them is still an open editorial question.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A programme announced, and two people removed
structure.summary: Richard sets out his intentions to the audience before anyone else appears, has Clarence sent to the Tower on a manufactured prophecy, and wins Lady Anne beside the corpse of the king he helped kill. Margaret arrives to curse everyone present, and the play files the curses for later use.

scenes.title: The winter of our discontent
scenes.summary: Richard explains the peace, his own body and his plan, then greets the brother he has just had arrested.

scenes.title: The wooing of Anne
scenes.summary: Interrupting Henry VI's funeral procession, Richard talks the dead king's daughter-in-law into accepting his ring.

scenes.title: Margaret's curses
scenes.summary: The old Lancastrian queen walks into a Yorkist quarrel and names the deaths that will follow, in order.

scenes.title: Clarence in the Tower
scenes.summary: Clarence describes a dream of drowning and judgement, then argues theology with the murderers his brother has sent.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A king dies and the peace he made dies with him
structure.summary: Edward IV has just reconciled his court when Richard tells him Clarence is dead, and the news kills him. The queen's relatives are arrested on the road, the citizens in the street can see what is coming, and the young heir is brought to London under escort by the man who intends to take his place.

scenes.title: The broken reconciliation
scenes.summary: Edward makes his court swear friendship; Richard announces Clarence's death and lets the guilt settle where it falls.

scenes.title: Three grieving women
scenes.summary: The Duchess of York, Queen Elizabeth and Clarence's children compete in mourning while Richard proposes a quiet escort for the prince.

scenes.title: Citizens in the street
scenes.summary: Three ordinary Londoners weigh a child king against ambitious kin and fear the worst.

scenes.title: Sanctuary
scenes.summary: News of the arrests at Pomfret sends the queen and the younger prince into sanctuary.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: The Tower, the council table and the pretended refusal
structure.summary: The princes are lodged in the Tower with courteous menace, Hastings is executed between one sentence and the next, and the crown is offered to a man who has rehearsed his reluctance with Buckingham beforehand. The theatre here is public and cynical, and the citizens' silence is part of the record.

scenes.title: The princes lodged
scenes.summary: The young Duke of York jokes about his uncle's shoulders; both boys are sent to the Tower for their safety.

scenes.title: Hastings ignores a dream
scenes.summary: Warned by Stanley's nightmare, Hastings decides that his standing with Richard makes him safe.

scenes.title: Pomfret
scenes.summary: Rivers, Grey and Vaughan are executed, and remember Margaret's curse as they go.

scenes.title: Strawberries and a head
scenes.summary: Richard asks for strawberries, leaves the council, returns accusing Hastings of witchcraft, and has him killed before dinner.

scenes.title: Managing the mayor
scenes.summary: Richard and Buckingham stage an emergency in rusty armour and explain the execution to the city.

scenes.title: The scrivener
scenes.summary: A clerk notes that the indictment of Hastings was written out before the man was accused.

scenes.title: The refusal
scenes.summary: Richard appears between two bishops and declines the crown twice before accepting it.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: The crown, and the first things it cannot buy
structure.summary: Richard is king by the middle of the act and immediately less interesting to himself: the soliloquies stop, Buckingham hesitates over the princes and is dropped, and Tyrrel does the work. The long fourth scene gives the stage to three women who have nothing left to lose, and to a second wooing that looks like the first and is not.

scenes.title: Shut out of the Tower
scenes.summary: The women are refused admission to the princes; Anne is summoned to be crowned and knows what it means.

scenes.title: Not in the giving vein
scenes.summary: Richard sounds Buckingham out about the princes, gets hesitation, and drops him mid-sentence.

scenes.title: Tyrrel's report
scenes.summary: The murder of the princes is described by a man who was not in the room, quoting men who were.

scenes.title: The women, and the second wooing
scenes.summary: Margaret teaches the other queens how to curse; Richard then asks Elizabeth for her daughter and believes he has won.

scenes.title: Stanley's message
scenes.summary: Stanley sends secret word to Richmond that his son is held hostage.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Two tents, eleven ghosts, and a horse
structure.summary: Buckingham goes to the block quoting the curse he brought on himself. On the eve of Bosworth the ghosts of everyone Richard has killed visit both tents in turn, cursing one sleeper and blessing the other. Richard wakes into the only soliloquy in which he cannot control who is speaking, and dies on foot.

scenes.title: Buckingham at Salisbury
scenes.summary: Led to execution on All-Souls' day, he recalls the oath he swore and the curse Margaret laid.

scenes.title: Richmond marches
scenes.summary: The invading earl describes the boar in the middle of England and counts his friends.

scenes.title: The night before Bosworth
scenes.summary: Two tents, two prayers, and eleven ghosts who speak the same words twice with opposite meanings.

scenes.title: A horse
scenes.summary: Unhorsed and seeking Richmond in the field, Richard offers his kingdom for a mount.

scenes.title: The two roses
scenes.summary: Richmond takes the crown, pardons the soldiers and announces a marriage that ends the civil wars.

characters.name: Richard, Duke of Gloucester
characters.summary: He is the funniest person in the play and knows it, which is the trap: the audience laughs at the jokes and is therefore in the room for the murders. He is not a hypocrite in the ordinary sense, because he tells us the truth constantly; he simply tells nobody on stage.
characters.clue: He is his own prologue, announces his plan in the first speech, and by Act V is arguing with himself about whether he is a villain and losing both sides.

characters.name: The Duke of Buckingham
characters.summary: The only person who is let into part of the plan, and he is good at it: the staged emergency and the bogus refusal of the crown are largely his productions. He hesitates exactly once, over the princes, and discovers that there was never a second place in the arrangement.
characters.clue: He boasts that he can counterfeit the deep tragedian, stage-manages a fake coronation appeal, and is dropped the moment he pauses over a murder.

characters.name: Queen Margaret
characters.role: Widow of Henry VI, survivor of the previous three plays
characters.summary: Historically she was not in England at all by this date, and Shakespeare keeps her anyway because the play needs someone who remembers. Her curses are not magic but memory with a very long reach, and the characters who dismiss her in Act I quote her accurately as they go to the block.
characters.clue: She has no title, no army and no business being there, and every death in the play happens in the order she names it.

characters.name: Queen Elizabeth
characters.role: Edward IV's widow, mother of the princes
characters.summary: She begins as a court politician anxious about her relatives' standing and ends as the one person who holds a long conversation with Richard and gives nothing away. Whether she agrees to give him her daughter or plays for time is a question the text leaves genuinely open.
characters.clue: She loses a husband, two sons and most of her family, then talks for two hundred lines with the man who took them and leaves him thinking he has won.

characters.name: Lady Anne
characters.role: Widow of Prince Edward, later Richard's queen
characters.summary: She is given one great scene, in which she out-argues Richard line for line and then takes his ring anyway, and one short scene four acts later in which she explains what the marriage has cost her. The play never accounts for the change, which is why the scene is still argued about.
characters.clue: She spits at him over a coffin, calls him a fouler toad than any poison ever hung on, and is wearing his ring before the corpse has been carried off.

characters.name: The Duchess of York
characters.role: Mother of Edward IV, Clarence and Richard
characters.summary: She has outlived a husband and is watching her sons destroy one another, and the play gives her the one curse that is delivered by someone with an unquestionable right to it. Her farewell to Richard is a mother's formal withdrawal of blessing, and he asks the drums to drown it.
characters.clue: Three of her sons appear in this play; she buries two of them and sends the third to Bosworth with her heaviest curse instead of a blessing.

characters.name: George, Duke of Clarence
characters.summary: He is imprisoned on the strength of a prophecy his brother invented and killed on the strength of a warrant his brother sent, and he spends his last scene describing a dream in which the dead he betrayed at Tewkesbury come for him. He is not innocent, and the murder is still shocking.
characters.clue: A letter of the alphabet sends him to the Tower, where he dreams of drowning among jewels and wakes to two men arguing about conscience.

characters.name: Lord Hastings
characters.summary: He celebrates the execution of his enemies in the morning and is executed himself after lunch, having explained an hour earlier that he knows Richard's face too well to be in danger. His speech on the block is the play's plainest statement about reading the powerful.
characters.clue: He laughs at a warning dream, rejoices at his rivals' deaths at Pomfret, and loses his head between the strawberries and dinner.
traits: briefly right about everything except himself

characters.name: The Earl of Richmond
characters.summary: He arrives with fewer than two hundred lines and no interior life at all, which is a choice rather than an oversight: after four acts of a man who talks to us constantly, the play offers a leader who talks only to his army and to God. The Tudor settlement is announced rather than dramatised.
characters.clue: He lands at Milford Haven, sleeps well, is blessed by every ghost that curses his opponent, and ends the play by marrying a woman who never appears in it.

themes.name: Tyranny as performance
themes.summary: Richard does not conceal power so much as dramatise it: a fake arrest, a fake emergency, a fake refusal of the crown, all played to audiences who are given their cues. The play argues that consent can be manufactured in public, in daylight, by people who know they are acting.
themes.development: Private improvisation in Act I becomes a civic production in 3.7, and collapses in Act V when there is nobody left to play to.

themes.name: The audience's complicity
themes.summary: Richard tells us his plans, invites us to admire the workmanship and jokes with us about the people he is about to kill. The discomfort is structural: the play gives the audience a better relationship with the murderer than it gives anyone on stage.
themes.development: The soliloquies stop once he is crowned, and the confidence is withdrawn precisely when the murders become unbearable.

themes.name: Curses, prophecy and memory
themes.summary: Margaret's curses in 1.3 function as a programme for the rest of the play, and the play's dead are its most reliable record-keepers. Whether this is providence or simply the way the guilty are made to remember is left unsettled.
themes.development: Named in Act I, quoted by Rivers at Pomfret, by Hastings on the block and by Buckingham at Salisbury, and finally embodied by the ghosts at Bosworth.

themes.name: Conscience
themes.summary: The word is argued over by two hired murderers before it ever troubles Richard, and their comic debate about the inconvenience of having a conscience sets the terms for his nightmare four acts later. He calls it a word cowards use, in a speech that is itself an attempt to talk himself out of one.
themes.development: A joke in 1.4, an absence through Acts II to IV, and by 5.3 a thousand several tongues, every one of them his.

themes.name: The women and formal lament
themes.summary: Four women who have every reason to hate each other end up sitting on the ground together, comparing dead sons in almost liturgical sequence. It is the one form of speech in the play that Richard cannot enter, interrupt or turn to his advantage.
themes.development: Rivalry in 1.3 and 2.2, shared grief in 4.1, and in 4.4 a set of matched laments that stop the plot for two hundred lines.

themes.name: History and legitimacy
themes.summary: The play inherits a Richard already blackened by Tudor chroniclers writing for the dynasty his defeat created, and it ends by announcing that dynasty as the end of civil war. Any reading has to hold both the play's theatrical delight in Richard and its political obligation to bury him.
themes.development: Yorkist triumph in 1.1, usurpation staged as election in 3.7, and in 5.5 a marriage that joins the roses and closes the sequence begun in the Henry VI plays.

techniques.name: Direct address
techniques.definition: A character speaking straight to the audience, treating them as confidants rather than observers.
techniques.inThisBook: Richard has the first word of the play and spends forty lines alone with us before the plot begins; the technique makes the audience an accessory before the fact.

techniques.name: Stichomythia
techniques.definition: Rapid exchange of single lines, each answering and turning the last.
techniques.inThisBook: The wooing of Anne and the later wooing of Elizabeth are both conducted as line-for-line duels, and the second one is where Richard's version of the trick stops landing cleanly.

techniques.name: Anaphora
techniques.definition: Beginning successive clauses with the same word or phrase.
techniques.inThisBook: Margaret's curses and the women's laments are built on hammered repetition — 'Thou that... Thou slander... Thou loathed' — which turns grief and hatred into something closer to ritual than conversation.

techniques.name: The Vice
techniques.definition: The joking, confiding tempter of the medieval morality plays, who explains his tricks to the audience as he performs them.
techniques.inThisBook: Richard names the inheritance himself in 3.1, comparing his own double meanings to 'the formal vice, Iniquity' — the play's clearest signal about where its hero's charm comes from.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The audience holding information a character on stage does not.
techniques.inThisBook: Because Richard briefs us in advance, almost every scene is watched from inside his plan: Clarence's trust, Hastings's confidence and the citizens' silence are all things we can price and they cannot.

techniques.name: Mirrored scenes
techniques.definition: Two scenes built to the same shape so that the second comments on the first.
techniques.inThisBook: Two wooings, two tents on the night before Bosworth, and eleven ghosts who deliver the same words twice with opposite force: the play thinks in matched pairs.

quotations.text: Now is the winter of our discontent Made glorious summer by this sun of York; And all the clouds that lour'd upon our house In the deep bosom of the ocean buried.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: The first lines of the play, spoken alone on an empty stage.
quotations.analysis: The famous first clause is only half a sentence, and the half that follows reverses it: the winter is over. 'Sun of York' is a pun on son and on Edward's badge, and the whole passage is a victory speech delivered by the one man in the family who has no use for victory.

quotations.text: Why, I, in this weak piping time of peace, Have no delight to pass away the time, Unless to spy my shadow in the sun And descant on mine own deformity
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: The middle of the opening soliloquy, explaining what peace leaves him to do.
quotations.analysis: 'Descant' is a musical term for improvising above a fixed melody, so his deformity is presented as a theme he performs variations on rather than a fact he suffers. The whole speech is his own account of his motives, which is exactly the reason to treat it with care.

quotations.text: And therefore, since I cannot prove a lover, To entertain these fair well-spoken days, I am determined to prove a villain And hate the idle pleasures of these days.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: The turn of the opening soliloquy, immediately before Clarence is led across the stage under guard.
quotations.analysis: 'Determined' carries both senses at once — resolved, and settled in advance by something outside him — and the play never chooses between them. Note also that the reasoning is theatrical rather than moral: he cannot get the lover's part, so he takes the other one.

quotations.text: Never hung poison on a fouler toad. Out of my sight! thou dost infect my eyes.
quotations.speaker: Lady Anne
quotations.context: Beside the coffin of Henry VI, answering Richard's compliment on her spitting.
quotations.analysis: She wins this exchange and every other one in the scene, which is what makes the ending of it so hard to explain away. Her images are all of contagion — poison, infection, basilisks — and by the end of the scene she has accepted a ring from the source.

quotations.text: Take up the sword again, or take up me.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: Kneeling with his breast bared, after Anne has let the sword fall.
quotations.analysis: One line, one repeated verb, two incompatible offers — and the staging does the arguing, since she must physically choose. He has converted a confession of murder into a proposal by making the only alternative another killing, which she has just refused to perform.

quotations.text: Was ever woman in this humour woo'd? Was ever woman in this humour won? I'll have her; but I will not keep her long.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: Alone, the moment Anne has left the stage.
quotations.analysis: Two rhetorical questions to us, and then the third line disposes of her in eleven words. The rhyme of woo'd and won makes the whole seduction sound like a completed piece of business, and the audience is being invited to applaud a performance whose victim has only just walked off.

quotations.text: Shine out, fair sun, till I have bought a glass, That I may see my shadow as I pass.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: The couplet that closes the wooing scene.
quotations.analysis: The shadow he could only 'descant on' in the first scene is now something he wants to look at, and he intends to buy a mirror to do it. Success has not altered how he sees his body; it has simply made him curious about the man who could pull this off.

quotations.text: Thou elvish-mark'd, abortive, rooting hog! Thou that wast seal'd in thy nativity The slave of nature and the son of hell!
quotations.speaker: Queen Margaret
quotations.context: Cursing Richard in front of the whole Yorkist court, which has been trying to ignore her.
quotations.analysis: 'Rooting hog' is his own badge, the white boar, turned into an insult, and 'seal'd in thy nativity' claims that his body was a signature written at birth. Richard's answer is to wait for her to finish and then substitute her name for his at the end of the curse — the only way anyone in the play ever interrupts her.

quotations.text: Why strew'st thou sugar on that bottled spider, Whose deadly web ensnareth thee about? Fool, fool! thou whet'st a knife to kill thyself.
quotations.speaker: Queen Margaret
quotations.context: To Queen Elizabeth, who has just tried to make peace in the quarrel.
quotations.analysis: Margaret is right about everything and heard by nobody, which is her function until Act IV, when Elizabeth comes to her to be taught this vocabulary. The same 'bottled spider' returns from Elizabeth's own mouth in 4.4, quoted almost exactly — the play keeps a record of who was listening.

quotations.text: And thus I clothe my naked villany With old odd ends stolen out of holy writ; And seem a saint, when most I play the devil.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: Alone after the quarrel scene, explaining his method to the audience.
quotations.analysis: He describes piety as a costume made of offcuts, and the verb 'play' places the whole performance in a theatre. This is a confession no other character will ever hear, and it arrives fifty lines after he has publicly forgiven his enemies for the injuries he invented.

quotations.text: Thus, like the formal vice, Iniquity, I moralize two meanings in one word.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: An aside, after telling the young prince that fame lives long without characters.
quotations.analysis: He names his own theatrical ancestry: the Vice of the morality plays, who joked with the audience while damning the hero. 'Moralize' means to draw out a meaning, and he is boasting that he can do it twice at once — one meaning for the boy, the other for us.

quotations.text: Off with his head! Now, by Saint Paul I swear, I will not dine until I see the same.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: At the council table, moments after asking the Bishop of Ely for strawberries.
quotations.analysis: The domestic detail is the horror: an execution is fitted into the gap before lunch, and the oath is sworn on a saint. Hastings has spoken one cautious conditional — 'if they have done this thing' — and the word 'if' is treated as the treason.

quotations.text: O momentary grace of mortal men, Which we more hunt for than the grace of God! Who builds his hopes in air of your good looks, Lives like a drunken sailor on a mast, Ready, with every nod, to tumble down Into the fatal bowels of the deep.
quotations.speaker: Hastings
quotations.context: On the way to the block, an hour after gloating over the executions at Pomfret.
quotations.analysis: The image is exact about what he got wrong: a sailor high on a mast can see further than anybody on deck and is still the first to fall. 'Nod' does double work — the roll of the ship and the small movement of a great man's head — so favour and shipwreck become the same gesture.

quotations.text: Tut, I can counterfeit the deep tragedian; Speak and look back, and pry on every side, Tremble and start at wagging of a straw, Intending deep suspicion
quotations.speaker: Buckingham
quotations.context: Answering Richard's question about whether he can act frightened, just before the mayor arrives.
quotations.analysis: Two men openly rehearse a piece of political theatre in front of the audience, and then perform it badly on purpose so that the citizens will believe it. 'Intending' here means stretching or pretending, and the vocabulary throughout is an actor's: counterfeit, tragedian, offices, stratagems.

quotations.text: I am not in the giving vein to-day.
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: Cutting off Buckingham, who has asked for the earldom he was promised.
quotations.analysis: One flat line of prose rhythm inside the verse ends a partnership that has run since Act I. 'Vein' is a mood and also a blood vessel, and the joke is that Buckingham has just declined to spill any; the alliance ends not in a quarrel but in a change of subject.

quotations.text: 'Lo, thus' quoth Dighton, 'lay those tender babes:' 'Thus, thus,' quoth Forrest, 'girdling one another Within their innocent alabaster arms: Their lips were four red roses on a stalk, Which in their summer beauty kiss'd each other.
quotations.speaker: Tyrrel
quotations.context: Reporting the murder of the princes, which he arranged but did not watch.
quotations.analysis: The play's most terrible act is reported at two removes, by a man quoting the murderers quoting each other, and the language is the prettiest in the play. 'Four red roses on a stalk' puts the Lancastrian emblem on two Yorkist children, which is the civil war reduced to the size of two sleeping boys.

quotations.text: Bloody thou art, bloody will be thy end; Shame serves thy life and doth thy death attend.
quotations.speaker: Duchess of York
quotations.context: The last words Richard's mother speaks to him, as he marches out to meet Richmond.
quotations.analysis: A rhymed couplet from a mother is a formal withdrawal of blessing, and the chiasmus of blood at either end of the first line makes his beginning and his end the same substance. He has had the drums sounded through her speech, so the audience hears it over noise he ordered.

quotations.text: Is the chair empty? is the sword unsway'd? Is the king dead? the empire unpossess'd? What heir of York is there alive but we?
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: On being told that Richmond is at sea, coming to claim the crown.
quotations.analysis: Four questions in two lines, all of them rhetorical, all of them asked by a man who took the chair by proving it was empty when it was not. He has become the legitimacy he used to dismantle, and the argument he now makes is the one his victims could have made against him.

quotations.text: What do I fear? myself? there's none else by: Richard loves Richard; that is, I am I. Is there a murderer here? No. Yes, I am: Then fly. What, from myself?
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: Waking in his tent at midnight after the ghosts have visited.
quotations.analysis: The soliloquy that was always a performance for us becomes a quarrel with no audience at all, and the syntax splits into question and answer as though two people were speaking. 'I am I' should be the most secure sentence in the language; here it is the last thing he can get to hold still.

quotations.text: My conscience hath a thousand several tongues, And every tongue brings in a several tale, And every tale condemns me for a villain.
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: The same speech, a few lines later.
quotations.analysis: The word he chose for himself in the first scene is now the verdict returned against him, and by a court made entirely of voices. Repetition of 'every' turns conscience into a crowd, which is the first time in the play that Richard is outnumbered in a room.

quotations.text: Conscience is but a word that cowards use, Devised at first to keep the strong in awe: Our strong arms be our conscience, swords our law.
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: Addressing his officers on the morning of Bosworth, a hundred lines after the nightmare.
quotations.analysis: He is arguing with the speech he made in the night, in public, in front of men who did not hear it. The claim that conscience was invented to control the powerful is a political theory, and he advances it a few hours before dying on a field where every ghost has voted the other way.

quotations.text: A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: Unhorsed in the field, hunting for Richmond among the decoys.
quotations.analysis: The most quoted line in the play is an offer to trade everything he has killed for back for a single animal, and it is spoken twice within seven lines, so the second time it is not rhetoric. Catesby offers to fetch a horse and Richard refuses, because what he wants is not escape but Richmond.

quotations.text: We will unite the white rose and the red: Smile heaven upon this fair conjunction, That long have frown'd upon their enmity!
quotations.speaker: Richmond
quotations.context: The closing speech, with the crown newly taken from Richard's body.
quotations.analysis: The settlement is announced rather than shown: the bride is a woman who never appears on stage and the peace is described in the future tense throughout. After five acts of a man who told the audience the truth and lied to everyone else, the play ends with a public statement nobody is invited to examine.

quotations.text: England hath long been mad, and scarr'd herself; The brother blindly shed the brother's blood, The father rashly slaughter'd his own son, The son, compell'd, been butcher to the sire
quotations.speaker: Richmond
quotations.context: Summing up the wars, a few lines before the play ends.
quotations.analysis: The lines summarise not just this play but the three Henry VI plays before it, and the father-and-son image is lifted almost directly from a scene in the last of them. The country is given a body that has been wounding itself, which is the only diagnosis the tetralogy offers for civil war.

timeline.label: Tewkesbury, and the death of Henry VI
timeline.detail: Two killings the play keeps returning to: Prince Edward at the battle and his father in the Tower.

timeline.label: Edward IV dies and Richard takes the throne
timeline.detail: The events of Acts II to IV are compressed from a few months of this year.

timeline.label: Bosworth Field
timeline.detail: Richard is killed on 22 August and Henry Tudor is crowned; the Wars of the Roses are conventionally dated from here to their end.

timeline.label: Thomas More's history of Richard III printed
timeline.detail: Written decades earlier and left unfinished, it supplied the Tudor chroniclers with the calculating, theatrical Richard Shakespeare inherited.

timeline.label: Holinshed's Chronicles reissued
timeline.detail: Shakespeare's immediate source, which carries More's account through Hall into the material of the play.

timeline.label: The True Tragedy of Richard the Third printed
timeline.detail: An anonymous play on the same story, evidence that Richard was already established stage material.

timeline.label: First quarto
timeline.detail: Printed by Valentine Simmes for Andrew Wise, and reprinted repeatedly over the next four decades.

timeline.label: Second quarto names Shakespeare
timeline.detail: The first of his plays to be widely reprinted in his lifetime carries his name from this edition onwards.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: A substantially different and longer text, printed among the histories.

timeline.label: Colley Cibber's adaptation
timeline.detail: A shortened rewriting that cut Margaret altogether and held the English stage for the best part of two centuries.

timeline.label: Garrick's debut as Richard
timeline.detail: The role made his name in London, and made the part an actor's proving ground.

timeline.label: Edmund Kean's Richard at Drury Lane
timeline.detail: A fast, unheroic reading that became the standard against which nineteenth-century Richards were measured.

timeline.label: Laurence Olivier's film
timeline.detail: Still using much of Cibber's shape, it fixed the opening soliloquy in the popular ear for a century of listeners.

timeline.label: Richard III's remains found in Leicester
timeline.detail: The skeleton showed severe scoliosis, reopening old arguments about how much of the play's body is Tudor invention.

places.name: The Tower of London
places.note: Clarence's cell, the princes' lodging, and the council chamber where Hastings is condemned.

places.name: London
places.note: The streets, the palace and Baynard's Castle, where Richard performs his refusal of the crown.

criticalViews.summary: The reading that takes Margaret's curses at face value: the play traces a pattern of retribution running back through the Henry VI plays and closing with the Tudor marriage, so that Richard is the instrument by which England is scourged and cleansed.
criticalViews.counter: It has to explain why the scourge gets the best lines, the jokes and the audience's attention for four acts.

criticalViews.summary: On this account the subject is the manufacture of consent: the staged arrest, the fake emergency at 3.5, the rehearsed refusal at 3.7, and the citizens who say nothing. Tyranny here works in public and depends on witnesses agreeing to be an audience.
criticalViews.counter: The last act abandons that interest almost completely for ghosts, dreams and a battle, which is a strange way to end a play about spin.

criticalViews.position: Richard as a role rather than a character
criticalViews.summary: Criticism has long treated the part as an inheritance from the morality-play Vice, a job of work for a virtuoso actor, which is why its stage history is a history of performers rather than of interpretations.
criticalViews.counter: It underrates 5.3, where the play insists on giving the role an interior at exactly the moment the performance stops.

criticalViews.position: Deformity, and who is doing the describing
criticalViews.summary: Disability criticism has examined how consistently the play lets Richard's body be read as a moral text — by Margaret, by the Duchess, and by Richard himself — and asked whether the play endorses that reading or exhibits it.
criticalViews.counter: Richard supplies most of the descriptions himself, which makes it hard to separate the play's view from his performance of one.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare make an audience enjoy the company of a murderer?
plan: Start with the structural fact: Richard speaks first, alone, and briefs us before the plot begins.
Analyse the jokes — the Vice comparison at 3.1, the two-meaning asides, the flat dismissal of Anne at 1.2.242.
Show how dramatic irony makes the audience an insider at every scene of trust, from Clarence to Hastings.
Mark the withdrawal: once Richard is crowned the soliloquies stop, and the murders arrive by report instead.
Conclude on 5.3, where he talks to himself because there is nobody else, and ask what the play has done to us by then.

essayQuestions.question: What is the function of the women in the play?
essayQuestions.focus: Lament, memory and the limits of Richard's method
plan: Begin with Margaret's anomalous presence: historically absent, dramatically indispensable as the play's memory.
Trace the curses of 1.3 through Rivers at Pomfret, Hastings on the block and Buckingham at Salisbury.
Read 4.4 as a formal set piece — matched laments, shared arithmetic of dead sons — that Richard cannot interrupt.
Compare the two wooing scenes, and weigh the case that Elizabeth is playing for time rather than consenting.
Decide whether the women are the play's moral centre or its chorus, and what difference that makes to the ending.

essayQuestions.question: 'The play is about theatre, not about history.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Performance, staging and the Tudor settlement
plan: Collect the play's own theatrical vocabulary: counterfeit, tragedian, vice, plot, induction, stratagem.
Analyse 3.5 and 3.7 as staged productions with scripts, props, cues and a silent audience of citizens.
Set against this the historical apparatus — the chroniclers, the tetralogy, the marriage that closes it.
Test the claim on Act V, which replaces performance with dreams, ghosts and a battle.
Conclude on Richmond, who makes a public statement no one is allowed to examine, and ask which mode wins.

essayQuestions.question: How far does the play invite sympathy for Richard?
plan: Open with the problem of evidence: nearly everything said about Richard's body is said by Richard or by his enemies.
Read the opening soliloquy as self-presentation rather than confession, noting 'descant' and 'determined'.
Weigh Margaret's and the Duchess's language against his own, and ask whether the play shares their view.
Examine 5.3 closely: the first speech in which he is not in control of who is talking.
Conclude on the difference between sympathy, fascination and complicity, and which of the three the play actually produces.

discussionQuestions: Richard tells us his plan in the first forty lines. Why is the play still suspenseful?
Anne accepts the ring of the man who killed her husband and her father-in-law. Is that scene believable, and does it need to be?
Margaret has no legal standing, no power and no business being in England. What does the play lose if a production cuts her, as many have?
The princes are murdered offstage and described in some of the play's loveliest language. Why that choice?
Richmond has almost no interiority at all. Is that a failure of the writing or a deliberate contrast?

related.why: Richard's first long soliloquy is there, and this play begins in the middle of a conversation started in it.
The other deposition play, and the opposite temperament: a king who cannot stop talking about himself and has no plan at all.
A later study of the same material — a usurper, a prophecy and a battlefield — with the jokes and the audience's company taken away.
Another history built around a child in the way of a crown, and a man who hesitates over the order to remove him.
The other Shakespearean study of a leader who understands that ruling is partly a performance, and is admired for it.
